generated.title: Where Will the Next Big One Hit? California vs Cascadia
generated.description:
Could two massive earthquakes strike America's West Coast close together in time? That's a hypothetical question, not a forecast.

Bay Area: the San Andreas is only one of many faults. The USGS Earthquake Outlook for the San Francisco Bay Region covers the whole regional fault system, including the Hayward-Rodgers Creek fault system, lesser-known faults and unknown faults. For 2014-2043 it puts the chance of at least one magnitude 6.7 or larger earthquake in the region at 72%. That is the 2014-2043 outlook period, not a new 30-year window starting today.

Cascadia: the Cascadia Subduction Zone lies off the Pacific Northwest coast. Its last great earthquake was on January 26, 1700, estimated at magnitude 8.7 to 9.2. The USGS 2025 Pacific Northwest fact sheet estimates a 10-15% chance of another approximately magnitude 9 earthquake in the next 50 years.

These two numbers cover different faults, magnitudes and time windows, so they are not directly comparable. No official source gives a probability for both regions having major earthquakes close together: that scenario is a hypothetical question, not a forecast. Scientists can't predict when the next big earthquake will strike; these are probabilities, not predictions.

Part of the Earthquake Science Explained series. Subscribe to Next Huge Quake for more earthquake science.
